question: What is the main goal of using isolation techniques in the hospital?

options.A: To prevent germs from spreading to others
options.B: To completely cure stubborn bacterial infections

explanation: You've got this! Isolation acts as a practical barrier to stop harmful pathogens from moving between patients, staff, and visitors. Simple and effective! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h1)

question: Who is usually the key person responsible for making sure isolation rules are followed on the ward?
explanation: Spot on! As nurses, we are right there at the bedside every day, making us the frontline champions for keeping infection control protocols active and correct. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h1)

question: In the chain of infection, which part is directly targeted when we use isolation precautions?

options.C: How the germ travels (mode of transmission)

explanation: Brilliant! Isolation barriers are specifically designed to block the highway that germs use to travel from one person or surface to another. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h2)

question: When a patient coughs and sends respiratory droplets into the air, what link in the infection chain does this show?
explanation: You're doing great! Respiratory droplets are the doorway (portal of exit) that allows the germ to leave the patient's body and travel outward. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h2)

question: Which group of patients should receive Standard Precautions?

options.B: Only patients in the surgical ward

explanation: Spot on! Standard Precautions are our baseline safety net. We treat every patient with these universal measures, no matter what their diagnosis is. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h3)

question: When do we add Transmission-Based Precautions to a patient's care?

options.A: Only after lab tests come back negative
options.B: During normal morning vital signs for healthy adults
options.C: When we want to stop washing our hands
options.D: When a patient has a known or suspected specific infection

explanation: Exactly! These are extra tools we bring out when we know or suspect a specific bug is present, used right alongside our standard precautions. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h3)

question: What kind of room airflow is needed for a patient who is on Airborne Precautions?
explanation: You got it! Negative pressure rooms act like a trap, keeping contaminated air inside and preventing it from flowing out into the hospital hallway. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h4)

question: A patient with suspected pulmonary TB is admitted. What protective mask must the nurse wear?
explanation: Well done! Because TB travels through tiny airborne particles, a basic surgical mask won't cut it—we need the tight fit and high filtration of an N95. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h4)

question: When removing your PPE after caring for a patient, which item should come off first?
explanation: Spot on! Your gloves are usually the dirtiest part of your PPE, so taking them off first stops you from accidentally spreading germs to clean surfaces. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h5)

question: What is the very first thing you must do before putting on a full set of PPE?
explanation: You're a star! Cleaning your hands is always step zero. It lowers the number of germs on your skin before you touch any clean gear. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h5)

question: What does 'cohorting' mean in an infectious disease unit?

options.A: Grouping patients with the same infection in one room
options.B: Putting healthy patients in recovery rooms
options.C: Isolating every single patient in a separate building
options.D: Sending infected patients to the outpatient clinic

explanation: Exactly! Cohorting is a clever way hospitals manage space by safely placing patients fighting the exact same bug together in one designated area. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h6)

question: Which of these is a good example of an engineering control in a hospital?

options.A: Written guidelines for giving oral meds
options.B: A nurse choosing to wear a face shield
options.C: A verbal reminder to wash your hands
options.D: Handwashing sinks placed right near ward entrances

explanation: Brilliant! Engineering controls are physical features built into the environment—like conveniently placed sinks—that make safe practices easy to do. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h6)

question: A patient in strict isolation feels very lonely and anxious. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Tell them that psychological stress has nothing to do with physical illness
options.B: Check in on them regularly with friendly conversation and reassurance
options.C: Inform them that visitors are banned forever
options.D: Only enter the room when giving medications

explanation: Spot on! A kind word, a friendly face, and regular check-ins go a long way in helping a patient feel less lonely and stressed during isolation. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h7)

question: What emotional challenge do patients placed on strict isolation precautions most commonly face?

options.B: Excitement to socialize with more people
options.C: Feelings of loneliness and feeling judged (stigmatization)

explanation: You got it! Being behind closed doors away from loved ones can make patients feel cut off, lonely, and emotionally distressed. Good nursing care keeps this in mind! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T15#GNS122_U2_T15_h7)
